data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism explicitly relies on verisimilitude as a selection criterion: 'Methodological selection based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness) and informational content rather than probabilistic induction.' The claim asserts this is 'defensible on Popper's terms.' However, Popper's own formal definition of verisimilitude was proven defective by Miller (1974) and Tichý (1974). On Popper's comparative definition, the ordering of false theories by truth-likeness collapses: any false theory that has more true consequences necessarily also has more false consequences, so no non-trivial comparison among false theories is possible. Since all scientific theories are, on Popper's view, false conjectures awaiting refutation, verisimilitude as Popper formally defined it cannot perform the comparative selection the mechanism requires. The claimed defensibility 'on Popper's terms' is thus undermined by a formal failure within Popper's own framework: the key concept invoked in the mechanism was refuted on the very terms the claim appeals to.
